Bottema

GeometryTrianglesConstructions
Game: Two squares share one corner of a triangle. Watch the orange dot: it is the middle of the line between two far corners of the squares.
How to play: Drag A, B or C with a mouse or finger, or focus a point and use the arrow keys. Press Show lines, Show hint and Check the claims to see why the dot stays put.
Look for the math

Build a square on each of two sides of a triangle. The far corners of those squares move as you drag the triangle's top corner, but the dot halfway between them does not. Bottema's theorem says that dot stays fixed.

The two squares

Start with triangle ABC. On side BC the square has far corners A_b and A_c; on side CA the square has far corners B_a and B_c. Each is made by a quarter rotation: A_b is C turned a quarter turn about B, and B_a is C turned a quarter turn the other way about A. The red line joins A_b to B_a, and the orange dot is its midpoint M.

Why C disappears

Write a quarter turn as R and the opposite turn as R⁻¹. Then A_b = B + R(C − B) and B_a = A + R⁻¹(C − A). Since a turn and its opposite undo each other, R(v) + R⁻¹(v) = 0. Adding the two far corners cancels every term with C in it:

M = (A_b + B_a) / 2 = (A + B) / 2 + R⁻¹(B − A) / 2.

Only A and B remain. The logic test checks this formula against the applet's own rotate-and-average calculation on 600 random positions, and checks that M stays put over a grid of 240 positions of C.

A right angle at M

The formula says M is the centre of the square built on AB. So MA = MB and the angle at M is a right angle: AMB is an isosceles triangle. The hint marks this right angle and puts matching tick marks on equal lengths; the other two far corners give a second right isosceles triangle, A_c M B_c.

The elementary proof

Drop perpendiculars from B_a, A_b, M and C onto AB. The right angles in the squares give B_aU = AZ and A_bV = BZ. The middle line of the trapezoid B_aUVA_b is therefore MW = (AZ + BZ) / 2 = AB / 2 — half the length of AB, independent of C. This is exactly the article's claim, and the logic test confirms it for tilted triangles too.

Try dragging C onto the line AB, then far away on the other side. The squares change completely, but M never moves.
